claims.text: feature-flags.md @ stage-4: a feature flag is a setting the code reads while running to choose between two paths, so a feature is deployed off and turned on later with no new deploy; the api has no flags at stage-4, the sample and the doc are the convention.

feature-flags.md: a release flag lives until its feature is on for every customer, then is removed with the old path; a kill switch turns off a costly feature under overload so placing/viewing orders keep running, stays for good, a form of graceful degradation; one flag, one kind.

feature-flags.md lines 72-74: feature code can reach production any day through the canary (ADR 0019) behind an off flag; the day the flag goes on is the release calendar's job (docs/team/release-calendar.md: fixed launch days, one at the end of each sprint), not the deploy's.

claims.text: FeatureFlags.IsOn (lines 25-30): percentage <= 0 -> false, >= 100 -> true, otherwise Bucket(name, customerId) < percentage. Bucket (lines 32-36): SHA-256 of UTF-8 "{flagName}:{customerId}", first 4 bytes as big-endian uint, % 100 -> 0..99.

BinaryPrimitives.ReadUInt32BigEndian reads the first four bytes of the span as a big-endian UInt32; SHA256.HashData returns the hash of its input, always 32 bytes, the same bytes for the same input. FeatureFlag (lines 10-15): Name, PercentOfCustomers; Off = 0, On = 100.
In .NET 10 a string's GetHashCode is not guaranteed to be stable: two runs of the same program may return different values; SHA-256 of the same bytes is the same on every run and machine.

claims.text: Since the flag is on when bucket < percentage and a customer's bucket is fixed, raising 10 -> 50 keeps buckets 0-9 and adds 10-49; lowering 10 -> 5 removes buckets 5-9 (every bucket below 5 is below 10).

feature-flags.md lines 47-60: release flags are raised by percentage of customers, not of requests (by request one customer sees the feature on and off); flag name is in the computation, so two flags at 10% do not land on the same group of customers.

A canary's HTTPRoute weights split requests, not customers, so one customer may reach both versions. Trade-offs table: merged code (branch or no flag) reaches a share of requests from the first canary step, everyone at 100; weight 0 turns it off during the steps.

claims.text: ADR 0019 chooses feature flags for changes customers see (canary for the api, rolling updates for Notifications and Payments).

Opinion (trade-offs, choices): no flag for a bug fix in an existing path when canary steps already limit exposure; a release flag when the launch day is chosen separately from the deploy; a kill switch, not a leftover release flag, for a feature that may need turning off under load.

feature-flags.md: turning a flag on changes a setting the running code reads, not the code, so no new build or deploy is needed; where Đơn Hàng will store flag settings is not decided at stage-4 and the lesson does not say.
